title: Dismissed on short shrift
primary_topics: SC's outright dismissal of Taguiwalo v. Duque (Sept. 1, 2020) seeking mandamus to compel COVID-19 mass testing
Doctrinal grounds: separation of powers (no judicial command of executive discretion) + mandamus extraordinary remedy + administrative exhaustion

Recent parallel dismissals: NAIA-renaming nullification; Gadon/OSG SALN requests targeting Justice Leonen
Beneficiaries of short shrift: Court, people, respondents, even petitioners, and the legal profession (shysters vs trustworthy)

stances.claim: The SC's outright 13-1-1 dismissal of Taguiwalo v. Duque (Sept. 1, 2020) -- without asking for respondent comment -- was correct on three independent grounds: (1) under separation of powers, courts 'cannot tell [officials] HOW to fulfill' duties that entail discretion or judgment; (2) mandamus 'cannot be availed of when a plain and speedy relief is available' and Executive Order No. 2, Series of 2016 was such a remedy; (3) petitioners 'have not shown they have exhausted administrative remedies before filing this case.'
stances.rhetorical_move: three-ground doctrinal defense of summary dismissal

stances.claim: The dismissal was not discriminatory or biased because the Court has applied the same short-shrift principle to other facially baseless petitions -- on Sept. 8 dismissing outright the petition to void the law renaming Manila International Airport as Ninoy Aquino International Airport on 'the same ground of facial inadequacy,' and on Sept. 15 summarily denying lawyer Larry Gadon's Sept. 7 letter and the OSG's Sept. 11 letter seeking Justice Leonen's SALNs (1990-2011) for a potential quo warranto proceeding.

These summary dismissals follow the Court's own Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2018) dictum to reduce backlog by dismissing 'plainly undeserving' pleas or those violating the hierarchy of courts, align with CJ Peralta's 10-point program (whose first item is 'Elimination of backlog in the Supreme Court'), and parallel the US Supreme Court's system of filtering out all facially defective petitions and deciding only 'a very limited number of truly meritorious cases.'
stances.rhetorical_move: tripartite-alignment ratification (own dictum + CJ program + Scotus model)

stances.claim: Short shrift benefits all stakeholders: the Court (more time and attention on crucial pending cases); the people ('justice delayed is justice denied' lament vanishes); the respondents (enjoy victory immediately without additional lawyers' fees); and even the petitioners (timely opportunities for alternative remedies -- Congress, executive officials, ballot, peaceful assemblies -- since 'not all problems can be solved by the judiciary'); and the legal profession (it 'differentiates shysters who take advantage of the gullibility of their clients from the trustworthy lawyers who elevate only truly worthy petitions').
Expect more short shrifts as the Court struggles to solve its backlog -- short shrift is a sustained institutional posture, not a one-off.

notable_anecdotes: The 13-1-1 vote on Taguiwalo v. Duque -- heavy supermajority for outright dismissal without comment, the procedural decisiveness that gave weight to the doctrinal grounds.
The 'cannot tell them HOW to fulfill them' formulation with capitalized HOW -- CJ's rare typographic emphasis preserved verbatim, marking the precise location of the separation-of-powers bar.
Three parallel September dismissals (Sept. 1 Taguiwalo, Sept. 8 NAIA-renaming, Sept. 15 Leonen-SALN-letters) -- clustered evidence that short shrift is institutional practice not selective targeting.

The 'I will await the Court's full resolution... and will thereafter write a column' parenthetical promise on the Leonen-SALN-Ombudsman question -- preview of a future column that signals CJ tracks this issue seriously.
Cross-referencing three prior CJ columns (4/7/19, 1/12/20, 8/23/20) -- making the present column part of a continuing series on backlog and SC management.

The five-stakeholder beneficiary enumeration -- Court, people, respondents, petitioners (with explicit list of alternative venues -- 'Congress... executive officials... the ballot... peaceful assemblies'), and legal profession -- exhaustive accounting that pre-empts critics.

The shyster-vs-trustworthy contrast deploying 'gullibility of their clients' against 'truly worthy petitions' -- language that pre-figures CJ's October 4 piece on prosecutors and shapes the legal-profession reform agenda.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban defends the Supreme Court's en banc outright dismissal of Taguiwalo v. Duque (Sept. 1, 2020) -- the petition for mandamus to compel the government to conduct COVID-19 mass testing -- against the 'brickbats' the dismissal provoked. Voting 13-1-1 without asking for respondent comment, the Court ruled that 'courts have no authority to issue writs of mandamus, no matter how dire the emergency, without a showing that an official of the executive branch failed to perform a mandatory, nondiscretionary duty.' CJ articulates the three independent doctrinal grounds: (1) under separation of powers, courts cannot order officials to perform jobs entailing 'discretion or judgment' -- while the judiciary can direct negligent officials to fulfill their duties, it 'cannot tell them HOW to fulfill them'; (2) mandamus is an extraordinary remedy that 'cannot be availed of when a plain and speedy relief is available,' and recourse to Executive Order No. 2, Series of 2016 was the plain, speedy, adequate remedy here; (3) petitioners failed to show exhaustion of administrative remedies. The Court was not discriminatory or biased: it has applied the same short-shrift principle elsewhere -- on Sept. 8 dismissing outright the petition to void the law renaming Manila International Airport as Ninoy Aquino International Airport on 'the same ground of facial inadequacy'; on Sept. 15 summarily denying Atty. Larry Gadon's Sept. 7, 2020 letter and the OSG's Sept. 11, 2020 letter requesting Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen's SALNs (1990-2011) 'to look into the possibility of initiating a quo warranto proceeding against Justice Leonen' (CJ promises a future column on the Ombudsman's new SALN-access guidelines). These summary dismissals follow the Court's own dictum in Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2018) to reduce backlog by dismissing 'plainly undeserving' pleas or those violating the hierarchy of courts; they align with CJ Peralta's 10-point program (whose first item is 'Elimination of backlog in the Supreme Court'); and they parallel the US Supreme Court's filtering system that decides 'only a very limited number of truly meritorious cases.' Short shrift benefits all stakeholders: the Court (more time for crucial pending cases); the people (the 'justice delayed is justice denied' lament 'would eventually vanish'); the respondents (immediate enjoyment of victory without additional lawyers' fees); the petitioners themselves (timely opportunities for alternative remedies -- Congress, executive officials, ballot, peaceful assemblies -- since 'not all problems can be solved by the judiciary'); and the legal profession, because it 'differentiate[s] shysters who take advantage of the gullibility of their clients from the trustworthy lawyers who elevate only truly worthy petitions, fully aware that patently worthless appeals would cause instant embarrassment for them and for their clients.' CJ closes: 'expect more short shrifts as the Court struggles to solve its backlog.'
